title: Apple Opens Health AI Study to Up to 200,000 iPhone Users
excerpt: The Apple Health AI Usage Study, built with OpenEvidence, will track how up to 200,000 US participants trust, understand and act on AI health answers over more than a year.
body:
• Apple has launched the Apple Health AI Usage Study in the United States, a virtual research study with its own app, run in collaboration with clinical AI platform OpenEvidence.
  • The study is open to up to 200,000 participants aged 21 and older who have an Apple Intelligence-enabled iPhone (iPhone 15 Pro or later) running iOS 26 or later.
  • Participants ask everyday health questions and get answers grounded in sources such as The New England Journal of Medicine, JAMA and Nature, with linked peer-reviewed citations.
  • To join, download the study app from the App Store and enroll in the app; Apple says study data will not be used to train AI models.

Apple on November 15 announced the launch of the Apple Health AI Usage Study, a virtual research study and dedicated app in the United States designed to examine how people interact with conversational health AI tools. Rather than shipping a health chatbot as a finished product, Apple says it wants to study what drives user trust, the quality of responses, how well people comprehend them, and what everyday health actions follow.

The study is conducted in collaboration with OpenEvidence, a clinical AI platform Apple describes as widely used by healthcare professionals. OpenEvidence generates answers using medical information from established sources including The New England Journal of Medicine, the Journal of the American Medical Association and Nature, and the study app shows linked, peer-reviewed clinical citations behind each response.

What participants actually do

Inside the app, participants can ask everyday health questions and explore complex medical information explained in approachable language, according to Apple. They can also choose to share HealthKit data types — such as resting heart rate, activity, sleep, or lab results — so the study can examine how personal data changes the relevance and understanding of answers. TechCrunch reported that users can rate the answers and give feedback on them, and will be asked to take part in monthly surveys; Apple aims to run the study for more than 12 months, TechCrunch said.

Apple says the study will also explore whether health AI can help participants prepare better for visits with their own doctors. The app includes safety guardrails intended to detect certain concerning questions and suggest the participant follow up with a provider or other resources.

"At Apple, we believe responsible innovation starts with scientific rigor and clinical grounding. Health is deeply personal, and conducting a dedicated research study is the most thoughtful way to understand how people engage with, comprehend, and evaluate health AI in everyday life."

— Sumbul Desai, M.D., Apple's vice president of Health and Fitness

Who can join

Enrollment is limited to the United States. Participants must be 21 or older and use an Apple Intelligence-enabled iPhone — an iPhone 15 Pro or later — running iOS 26 or later. The study is open to up to 200,000 participants, and joining is done through the study app itself, which Apple has made available to download from the App Store.

Privacy terms

Apple says the study was designed with privacy protections, transparency and clinical guardrails, and that study data will not be used to train AI models. Participants keep control over whether to share any HealthKit metrics or survey responses. TechCrunch reported that data is anonymized before it is sent to a secure third-party cloud provider, and that OpenEvidence deletes query and response data after 24 hours.

Why Apple is studying this first

The demand Apple is probing is already large. OpenAI said earlier this year that its users were asking more than 300 million health-related queries each week, TechCrunch reported. Apple notes that consumer health tools powered by large language models can at times give responses that are incomplete or unclear, which it says is why research into presenting health information with greater clarity is needed.

"Patients and clinicians are both turning to AI, but the tools they use are being built and tested in separate worlds," said Robert M. Wachter, M.D., professor and chair of the Department of Medicine at UCSF, in Apple's announcement. "When patients and doctors draw on versions of the same trustworthy tools, patients arrive prepared, conversations improve, and next steps happen seamlessly."

Apple has not said whether AI-powered answering will come to its Health app or Siri, TechCrunch noted. For now the study is US-only, so diaspora readers in the United States with a recent iPhone can enroll, while readers in India and elsewhere cannot join this study. Apple is explicit about the boundary of the tool itself: the study app is not meant to diagnose or treat any condition, or to replace the advice of medical professionals.
